chapters.name: Chapter 1: Leading and planning with AI

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What AI can do for a community group
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: List three time-consuming tasks in your group that AI could help with.
This lesson builds toward: Given the tasks your group does each month, you will identify which ones AI can help draft and which need people, naming at least three tasks for AI and the human work it frees time for.
Community leaders spend hours writing flyers, emails, meeting notes, sign-up lists and reports. A free AI assistant such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot or Google Gemini can draft these in minutes.
AI is good at first drafts, summaries, checklists, schedules, translating a flyer into plain words, and brainstorming ideas. It is not good at knowing your neighbors, judging what your community really needs or keeping private stories safe.
A good leader uses AI to free up time for the human work: listening, building trust and showing up.
Words to know:
- Nonprofit: an organization that serves a mission instead of making profit for owners.
- Draft: a first version you will improve.
Try it now: Write down three tasks that take your group the most time each month. Next to each, write how AI could help with a first draft.
You can now spot tasks in your group that AI can speed up, and the ones that need people.

check.q: Which is AI good at for a community group?
options: Writing a first draft of meeting notes
check.why: AI is good at drafts and summaries; people know the community.

check.q: AI saves you three hours a week on paperwork. What is the best use of that time?
options: Listening to families and building trust
Letting AI talk to families for you
check.why: Leaders use AI to free time for human work like listening and showing up.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: A clear mission and a measurable goal
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a one-sentence mission and one measurable goal with AI's help.
This lesson builds toward: Given what your group does, you will write a one-sentence mission and one measurable goal with AI's help, edited with your team so it says who, what and why, and the goal can be counted by a date.
A mission says why your group exists in one sentence: who you serve, what you do and why it matters. Example: "We make sure no family on the East Side goes hungry by running a weekly free food pantry."
A goal says what you will achieve and by when, in a way you can count. "Help more people" is not measurable. "Serve 150 families a month by June" is.
Ask AI: "Here is what our group does: [describe]. Write three one-sentence mission statements in plain words, and two measurable goals for the next six months." Then choose and edit with your team so the words sound like your community.
Step by step:
- Describe who you serve, what you do and why.
- Ask AI for three mission options and two measurable goals.
- Choose one of each with your team.
- Edit so it sounds like your community.
Words to know:
- Mission: one sentence that says why your group exists.
- Measurable goal: a goal you can count and check by a date.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant for three mission statements and two measurable goals for your group. Pick one of each and edit them in your own words.
You can now write a clear mission and a measurable goal for your group.

options: You can count it by a date
check.why: A measurable goal says what you will achieve and by when, in a way you can count.

check.q: AI's mission statement uses words your members would never say. What do you do?
options: Ask AI for a longer one
Edit it with your team so it sounds like your community
check.why: The mission should sound like your community, so you edit it together.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Planning a program or event with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to make a simple timeline and task list for a program or event.
This lesson builds toward: Given a program or event goal, you will create a timeline and task list with AI, adding what AI missed and putting a name and date by every task.
Once you have a goal, plan the work. AI can turn a goal into a timeline (what happens when) and a task list (who does what).
Example prompt: "We are holding a back-to-school supply giveaway for 100 kids on August 10 at the community center. Make a simple 6-week timeline and a task list with three volunteer roles. Use short sentences."
Review it with your team. Remove steps that do not fit your community, add what AI missed (like permits, translation or rides for elders), and put a name and date by each task.
Step by step:
- Give AI the event, the date, the place and how many people.
- Ask for a timeline and a task list.
- Review it with your team and add what is missing.
- Put a name and a date by each task.
Words to know:
- Timeline: a list of what happens when, in order.
- Task list: a list of jobs with who will do each one.
Try it now: Ask AI for a timeline and task list for one program or event your group could hold. Add one thing AI missed and put a name by each task.
You can now turn a goal into a timeline and task list with AI and your team.

options: A list of who does what
check.why: A task list shows each job and who will do it.

check.q: AI's plan for a cookout does not mention a permit for the park. What do you do?
options: Add checking the permit to the task list with a name and date
Ask AI to apply for it
check.why: You add what AI missed, like permits, and give the task an owner and date.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Organizing volunteers, and keeping everyone safe
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write clear volunteer role descriptions and safety steps.
This lesson builds toward: Given the volunteer jobs in your plan, you will write short volunteer role descriptions and the safety steps they need, following your organization's policy when minors or vulnerable adults are involved and using no real names in AI.
Volunteers stay when they know what to do. AI can write short role descriptions: what the job is, how long it takes, what skills help and who to ask for help. It can also draft a sign-up message and reminder texts.
If your program serves children or vulnerable adults, safety comes first. Common practices include background checks for volunteers, a rule that two adults are present instead of one adult alone with a child, and clear rules for phone and social media contact. Follow your organization's policy and any state rules, and ask your insurer or a lawyer if you are unsure.
Keep volunteer and client information private. Do not paste names, phone numbers or personal stories into AI tools; use roles and placeholders instead.
Step by step:
- Ask AI for short role descriptions for each volunteer job.
- Add safety steps if minors or vulnerable adults are involved.
- Follow your organization's policy and state rules.
- Use placeholders, never real names or numbers, in AI prompts.
Words to know:
- Background check: a check of a person's records before they work with children or vulnerable people.
- Two-adult rule: a common safety practice: at least two adults are present with children, never one alone.
- Vulnerable adult: an adult who may need extra protection, such as some elders or people with disabilities.
Try it now: Ask AI to write three short volunteer role descriptions for your plan. If minors are involved, add the safety steps your organization requires.
You can now write clear volunteer roles and include the safety steps your group needs.

check.q: What should a volunteer role description include?
options: What the job is, how long it takes and who to ask for help
check.why: Clear roles say what to do, how long and who to ask.

check.q: You want AI to draft a reminder text for volunteers. What do you paste in?
options: Every volunteer's name and phone number
The role, date and time, using placeholders for names
check.why: Use roles and placeholders, never real names or numbers, in AI prompts.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Finding grants and writing a grant summary
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Find one grant opportunity and draft a five-sentence summary of your project.
This lesson builds toward: Given a project that needs money, you will find one grant opportunity and draft a five-sentence grant summary with AI, with every fact matching your records and the funder's rules followed.
Grants are money given for a purpose that you do not pay back. Local sources often fit small groups best: community foundations, local businesses, banks, faith groups and city or county programs. Your library may offer free grant research help.
Grants.gov lists federal grants. Most of them are for organizations, not individuals, and none give personal financial help. Applying through Grants.gov requires registering your organization, which takes time, so read the registration steps on Grants.gov and start early.
AI can help you write a short project summary: the need, what you will do, who it helps, your measurable goal and the amount you are asking for. Every fact and number must be true and match your records. Read the funder's rules and use their questions, word limits and deadline.
Step by step:
- Ask your library or community foundation about local grants.
- Search Grants.gov if your organization is ready for federal grants.
- Ask AI for a five-sentence summary: need, plan, who it helps, goal, amount.
- Check every fact and follow the funder's rules.
Words to know:
- Grant: money given for a purpose that you do not pay back.
- Funder: the group or agency that gives the grant.
- Community foundation: a local charity that gives grants to groups in its area.
Official sources:
- Grants.gov: Grant eligibility
Try it now: Find one grant your group could apply for (local or on Grants.gov). Ask AI to draft a five-sentence summary of your project, then check every fact.
You can now find a grant opportunity and draft an honest project summary.

options: Money for a purpose that you do not pay back
check.why: A grant is money given for a purpose, not paid back.

check.q: A funder allows 100 words, and AI wrote 180. What do you do?
options: Cut it to fit the funder's 100-word limit
check.why: Follow the funder's rules, including word limits.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Updating supporters and setting AI rules for your group
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a supporter update and five simple AI rules for your group.
This lesson builds toward: When you share results and use AI as a group, you will write a supporter update and five simple AI rules for your group, using stories only with written permission and keeping decisions about people in human hands.
Supporters give again when they see results. AI can turn your numbers into a short, warm update: "This month we served 142 families and gave out 300 backpacks. Thank you!" Share stories only with written permission, and change names if the person wants.
Every group that uses AI should agree on a few simple rules. For example: 1) Never put names, addresses, phone numbers, health or immigration details of the people we serve into AI. 2) A person reads and checks everything before it goes out. 3) We do not let AI make decisions about who gets help. 4) We tell people when a message was mostly written by AI if they ask. 5) We use only approved, free or donated tools.
Write your rules down, share them with volunteers and review them once a year.
Step by step:
- Ask AI to turn your results into a short thank-you update.
- Use stories only with written permission.
- Write five AI rules with your team.
- Share the rules with volunteers and review them yearly.
Words to know:
- Supporter: someone who gives time, money or help to your group.
- Policy: a written set of rules your group agrees to follow.
Try it now: Final task: put it together in a one-page program plan: mission, measurable goal, timeline, three volunteer roles with safety steps, a five-sentence grant summary and your group's five AI rules. Remove anything private before sharing.
You can now lead a community project with a clear plan and safe, honest AI use.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Mission and goal No mission, or the goal cannot be counted. One-sentence mission with who, what and why, and one goal with a number and a date. Edited with the team so it sounds like the community. Timeline No timeline, or tasks without names or dates. A simple timeline with a name and date by every task. Includes something AI missed, such as permits, translation or rides. Volunteer roles and safety Fewer than three roles, or no safety steps when minors are involved. Three clear roles, with the organization's safety steps where needed. Roles say how long the job takes and who to ask for help. Grant summary Missing parts, or facts that do not match records. Five sentences: need, plan, who it helps, goal and amount, all checked. Fits a real funder's word limit and questions. AI rules and privacy Fewer than five rules, or private information left in the plan. Five clear AI rules, and no private information in the plan. Rules include a yearly review and are ready to share with volunteers. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: When can you share a family's story in an update?
check.why: Stories are shared only with written permission.

check.q: A board member suggests letting AI choose which families get help first. What does your AI rule say?
options: No; people make decisions about who gets help
check.why: AI does not make decisions about who gets help; people do.
